# Actor Pool

**Actor Pool** is a Rust library implementing a round-robin load-balanced pool of homogeneous actors, distributing work evenly across N worker instances with O(1) per-dispatch selection.

## Why It Matters

When multiple identical worker actors process incoming requests, naive random selection creates uneven load distributions — some workers build up queues while others sit idle. Round-robin scheduling eliminates this variance: each worker receives exactly 1/N of the total load (±1 message at any moment). This is the same principle behind TCP connection pooling, database read-replica distribution, and Kubernetes service load-balancing. In actor systems, pooling is essential when individual actors are single-threaded (processing one message at a time), so throughput scales linearly with pool size only if load is distributed evenly.

## How It Works

The pool maintains a `VecDeque<T>` of actor references and a `next: usize` counter. On each `next()` call:

```
idx = next % actors.len()    // O(1) modular arithmetic
next = next.wrapping_add(1)  // O(1), avoids overflow on long runs
return &actors[idx]
```

Using `wrapping_add` ensures the counter never panics on overflow, even in a system running for months with billions of dispatches. The modular wrap means each actor is selected in strict rotation.

**Fairness analysis:** After k dispatches, actor i has received either ⌊k/N⌋ or ⌈k/N⌉ messages. The maximum imbalance between any two actors is exactly 1 at all times — perfect fair sharing.

**Comparison with alternatives:**

| Strategy | Load Balance | State | Hot Spots |
|----------|-------------|-------|-----------|
| Round-robin | Perfect (±1) | Counter only | None |
| Random | σ ≈ √(k/N) | None | Possible |
| Least-loaded | Perfect | Per-actor queue sizes | Requires monitoring |
| Consistent hash | Key-dependent | Hash ring | Skewed keys |

Round-robin is optimal when all actors have equal processing speed and all requests have equal cost. When processing times vary, least-loaded scheduling outperforms, at the cost of per-actor state tracking.

## Quick Start

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut pool: ActorPool<i32> = ActorPool::new();
    pool.add(1);
    pool.add(2);
    pool.add(3);
    assert_eq!(*pool.next().unwrap(), 1);
    assert_eq!(*pool.next().unwrap(), 2);
    assert_eq!(*pool.next().unwrap(), 3);
    assert_eq!(*pool.next().unwrap(), 1); // wraps around
}
```

## API

| Method | Signature | Complexity |
|--------|-----------|------------|
| `new` | `() → Self` | O(1) |
| `with_capacity` | `(usize) → Self` | O(1) |
| `add` | `(T) → ()` | O(1) amortized |
| `next` | `() → Option<&T>` | O(1) |
| `len` | `() → usize` | O(1) |
| `is_empty` | `() → bool` | O(1) |

## Architecture Notes

Actor Pool implements the **load-distribution layer** within the SuperInstance fleet's actor system. In the γ + η = C conservation equation, the pool ensures that computational load (γ) is evenly distributed across available workers, preventing thermal hotspots and ensuring conservation-law verifications run in parallel without stragglers.

See [ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/SuperInstance/SuperInstance/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md).

**Variation analysis:** Under Poisson arrivals with rate λ, the actual number of messages received by each worker follows a binomial distribution B(k, 1/N). The coefficient of variation is CV = √((N−1)/(k+1)) × 1/√N, which approaches 0 as k grows — convergence to perfect fairness. For N = 10 workers and k = 1000 dispatches, the maximum imbalance is at most 1 (by the round-robin invariant).

**When round-robin fails:** Round-robin assumes uniform processing cost. When workloads are heterogeneous (some requests take 100× longer), a single slow request can stall one worker while others idle. In this case, **work-stealing** (idle workers steal from busy workers' queues) provides better throughput at the cost of per-worker queue state and lock contention. Work-stealing is O(1) amortized per steal and achieves near-optimal load balancing with high probability.
